purpose: How a managed Wi-Fi provider turns network design, installed access points and continuing care into one accountable subscription product, decides which venue classes (restaurant, motel and small lodging, office, retail shop, multi-dwelling property) to sell it to, chooses whether the guest-experience or the operations-dependence story carries the recurring fee, builds the per-site and per-access-point price from its own verifiable cost inputs, states what the monthly service includes and excludes and where the internet provider's responsibility ends, positions honestly against one-time installers, and decides which deals to decline before any survey or design work begins.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors

site facts that decide coverage, cabling and cost (construction materials, existing conduit and closet space, ceiling and mounting conditions, circuit type and demarcation location, neighbouring radio congestion, peak device counts) are unknown until surveyed and are carried as pending facts, never as assumptions dressed up as promises

pricing is expressed as a mechanism: per-site and per-device components assembled from cost inputs the provider itself holds (vendor licence quotes, its own loaded labour rate, spare stock, insurance, travel), so any figure is reconstructable and re-verifiable per deal rather than quoted as a market rate

licensing, permitting, lease-consent, franchise-standard and consumer-privacy duties vary by jurisdiction, landlord and brand and change over time; each is named as an obligation class to verify currently and locally before it is sold
the provider sells its own accountable service; internet carriers, equipment manufacturers and point-of-sale or property-system vendors remain third parties whose terms are read per deal, not assumed
the material is operator education for someone running this business; it is not personalized legal, tax, financial or insurance advice for the provider or the venue
exclusions: RF site-survey execution, access-point placement, channel and power planning, and post-install validation testing — the design and deployment knowledge base owns those

SSID and VLAN segmentation design, captive-portal build and configuration, hardware platform and cloud-controller selection, cabling and installation practice, and documentation handoff — the design and deployment knowledge base owns those

remote monitoring and alerting operations, firmware and patch execution, service-level target design and uptime reporting, support-tier operations and escalation runbooks, renewal and retention plays, and expansion into additional sites or adjacent services such as cameras and voice — the monitoring, management and service-level operations knowledge base owns those
any interception, inspection, logging of content, resale or brokerage of guest traffic or guest personal data, and any monetization of sign-in page data beyond a disclosed, consented, venue-owned use

invented figures of any kind — prices, monthly fees, referral amounts, margins, market sizes, uptime percentages or revenue-lift statistics stated as fact rather than as a mechanism or an explicitly measured result
jurisdiction-specific licensing, permit, tax and privacy rule detail; obligation classes are named and the reader is told to verify current rules in their jurisdiction
personalized financial, legal, tax or insurance advice to the provider or to the venue

competency_questions.question: What exactly is a managed Wi-Fi provider selling, and why does a monthly fee exist at all rather than a single installation price?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: MANAGED_WIFI_PRODUCT_THESIS names the three bundled components and the accountable outcome, and SERVICE_SCOPE_AND_TIERS lists the standing monthly activities the fee performs even in a month when nothing breaks

competency_questions.question: Which venue classes should this provider pursue, who signs in each, and what is each class actually buying Wi-Fi for?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: VENUE_CLASS_TAXONOMY gives per class the signing role, the demand trigger, the footprint driver and a disqualifier, and GUEST_VS_OPS_VALUE_SPLIT says which value story that class responds to

competency_questions.question: For a specific venue, does the guest-experience story or the operations-dependence story carry the recurring fee, and how is each told without exaggeration?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: OPS_DEPENDENCY_DISCOVERY supplies the venue's own inventory of what breaks when the network drops, GUEST_VS_OPS_VALUE_SPLIT chooses the load-bearing story from it, and HONEST_CLAIM_DISCIPLINE bounds the language to evidenced statements with no invented loss figures

competency_questions.question: What must the offer promise about guest and resident data, what may a sign-in page collect, and what is refused outright?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: GUEST_DATA_PRIVACY_PROMISE states the no-interception and no-resale commitments, the disclosure-first collection rule and who owns collected data, and MDU_VENUE_SHAPE extends it to resident traffic in multi-dwelling properties with the obligation class flagged for local verification

competency_questions.question: How is the monthly price for a given venue built from per-site and per-access-point components without inventing figures, and how is a quoted number verified per deal?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PRICE_MECHANISM_ARCHITECTURE names the per-site and per-device components, the modifiers and the documents each cost input is read from, and OFFER_UNIT_ECONOMICS shows the check that the resulting price funds the service actually promised

competency_questions.question: Who buys the equipment, who owns it, how is its cost recovered, and what happens to it and to the configuration if the subscription ends?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HARDWARE_COST_RECOVERY_MODEL sets out the purchase, amortised and provider-owned options with their cancellation consequences, and CONTRACT_TERM_AND_EXIT states the term, renewal, notice and the handover of credentials, configuration and documentation on exit

competency_questions.question: What is inside the monthly scope, what is billable extra, and where does the internet carrier's responsibility end and the provider's begin?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SERVICE_SCOPE_AND_TIERS lists inclusions, exclusions and how tiers differ, and RESPONSIBILITY_BOUNDARY_MAP fixes the circuit, managed-network and application boundaries plus what triage the provider performs across them

competency_questions.question: Which facts about a venue must wait for a survey, and what may be said about coverage and performance before that survey happens?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SITE_FACT_QUALIFICATION enumerates the survey-pending facts and the assumption-plus-contingency form they take in a quote, and HONEST_CLAIM_DISCIPLINE gives the conditional language permitted before measurement

competency_questions.question: How does the shaped offer differ between a restaurant, a motel, a multi-dwelling property, and an office or retail shop?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: RESTAURANT_VENUE_SHAPE, LODGING_VENUE_SHAPE, MDU_VENUE_SHAPE and OFFICE_RETAIL_VENUE_SHAPE each name that class's buyer, load-bearing systems, coverage driver, support-hours reality and the shaping decision that follows

competency_questions.question: How does the provider position against a one-time installer or a consumer router without disparaging anyone or overstating its own record?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: INCUMBENT_SITUATION_AUDIT establishes what the venue actually has, ONE_TIME_INSTALLER_POSITIONING draws the structural contrast in terms of who owns which duty, and PROOF_ASSET_DISCIPLINE limits the supporting evidence to assets the provider can produce on demand

competency_questions.question: Which licensing, consent and code obligation classes must be settled before selling installation-plus-management work, and who holds each?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: LICENSING_OBLIGATION_CLASSES names each class with a holder decision (in-house, subcontracted or the venue's own) and the instruction to verify current rules in the venue's jurisdiction, and DEAL_FIT_SCREEN treats an unresolvable class as a decline condition

competency_questions.question: Where do qualified venue leads come from, and how are partner and referral arrangements kept clean and disclosed?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PARTNER_LEAD_CHANNELS lists the channels where venue Wi-Fi pain is already visible and states the written terms, account ownership and disclosure duty attached to a referral fee, with the obligation class flagged for verification

competency_questions.question: When should a deal be declined, and what must a signable proposal contain before design and installation work begins?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DEAL_FIT_SCREEN lists the recurring disqualifiers and the recorded-decline practice, and PROPOSAL_AND_SURVEY_GATE names every element the signable document must carry and the gate conditions that let it pass to design

competency_questions.question: How does the provider know it can actually service a venue at the tier and price it is about to quote, and when does growth outrun capacity?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: OFFER_UNIT_ECONOMICS estimates the recurring work a site of this shape generates against the price after licence, spares, insurance and travel, and asks the portfolio question of how many such sites one technician can hold before the promised response breaks

glossary.definition: A bundled product in which one provider designs a venue's wireless network, supplies and installs the equipment, and then charges a monthly fee to keep it working — watching it, updating it, changing it and answering the venue's staff — so that responsibility for 'is the Wi-Fi working?' sits with a named company rather than with whoever set it up.

The ceiling- or wall-mounted radio unit that serves client devices; the count of access points at a venue is driven by walls, materials, room layout and peak device load rather than floor area alone, and it is the most common per-device unit in a managed subscription.

A price structure in which the monthly fee is composed of a standing per-site component (the cost of holding a location: management platform licence, monitoring, support rota, reporting, travel radius) plus a per-device component for each managed access point, switch or gateway, with modifiers for support hours and included onsite visits.

The two logically separate services carried over the same infrastructure: the network offered to customers, guests or residents, and the network the venue's own revenue-critical systems use (card terminals, point-of-sale, kitchen screens, scanners, property-management and lock systems, cameras, cloud phones). They generate different value stories and different tolerance for downtime.

The sign-in page a guest sees before being allowed onto a guest network; it may present terms, a splash screen or a data-entry form. Whatever it collects must be disclosed plainly to the guest and belongs to the venue, and building or configuring it belongs to the design and deployment knowledge base, not to this one.

The physical point where the internet carrier's responsibility ends and the venue's inside wiring and equipment begin; its location and type decide where the managed network starts, who is accountable during an outage, and often how much cabling a deal needs.

The predictable subscription income a provider holds across its book of sites, as distinct from one-time installation revenue; it is the quantity a managed offer is designed to build, and it is only real to the extent the provider can service the sites that generate it.

An onsite visit by a technician, with its drive time, vehicle cost and lost bench hours; whether truck rolls are included, capped or billed is one of the few honest dimensions along which subscription tiers differ, and travel distance is a real input to whether a venue can be served at all.

The onsite measurement pass that establishes what the building actually does to a wireless signal and what cabling and mounting are possible; in this knowledge base it appears only as the event that converts pending site facts into firm ones, with its execution owned by the design and deployment knowledge base.

An apartment, condominium or mixed-tenant building where the buyer is a property manager or owner but the users are residents or tenants; deals turn on whether coverage is common-area or in-unit, who supports the resident, what the building's existing internet arrangement is, and written owner consent for risers and shared spaces.

nodes.definition: State plainly what is being sold, because everything downstream inherits it: not a carton of access points and a day of labour, but a continuing service in which one company owns the question 'is the Wi-Fi working?' for a venue. The product fuses three things venues normally buy separately — a network designed for this building and this device load, the equipment that implements that design, and a monthly subscription under which the provider watches the network, keeps configuration and firmware current, answers staff when something breaks, makes changes as the venue changes, and reports on what it did. The thesis fixes where the durable margin lives (the subscription, not the hardware markup), why a buyer accepts a recurring charge (they are buying an owner of the problem, not a device), and what the provider is therefore obliged to perform every month even when nothing has failed.

included: the three bundled components sold as one accountable service
the reason a recurring fee exists and what it buys
the standing monthly obligation the provider takes on
excluded: how the network is designed and where access points go
monitoring tooling, alert handling and service-level targets
equipment platform selection

pros.claim: Selling an outcome instead of equipment converts a one-off install into a book of recurring revenue that survives the next hardware refresh
pros.example: a restaurant that bought a router once in a big-box store and was never seen again becomes a site under monthly care with a named owner and a documented configuration

pros.claim: A single accountable party is the thing venue operators actually want, and it is hard for a box seller to copy
pros.example: a motel manager who currently calls three vendors during an outage gets one number and a triage promise instead

cons.claim: The recurring promise is a standing obligation that must be staffed and funded whether or not anything breaks that month
cons.example: a quiet month still consumes management-platform licences, spare stock, insurance and an on-call rota

failure_modes: describing the product as hardware plus installation, so the buyer reads the monthly fee as an unexplained surcharge
promising the outcome in conversation ('it will always work') while the scope actually sold is only monitoring
letting hardware markup become the profit centre so the subscription is priced too thin to fund the service
acceptance_tests: the written service definition names the three bundled components, states the accountable outcome in one sentence, and lists at least three things the provider performs every month when nothing is broken
revisit_triggers: the bundled components or the service catalogue change
buyers repeatedly ask what the monthly fee is actually for, which means the thesis is not landing

base.update_signal: the bundle of components sold, or the monthly obligation attached to the fee, is restated

nodes.definition: Sort the addressable market into venue classes that behave differently as buyers rather than treating 'small business Wi-Fi' as one market. For each class the provider writes down who signs (owner-operator, general manager, property manager, office manager, franchisee), what the network is load-bearing for, what drives the access-point count in that class (dining and service areas, guest rooms and corridors, unit doors and common areas, desks and stockroom), when money becomes available (seasonal trade, renovation and franchise refresh cycles, lease renewals, tenant turnover), how fast the class decides, who else must consent, and what typically disqualifies a site. That map is what makes a repeatable offer possible: a class with a known buyer, a known trigger and a known shape can be quoted from a structure, while an unclassified venue has to be engineered and argued from scratch every time.

included: the classes worth serving and their signing roles
demand triggers and buying cycles per class
footprint and consent drivers per class
class-level disqualifiers
excluded: the tailored offer for a specific class, which the venue-shaping units carry
the individual site's measured facts

pros.claim: A named buyer and trigger per class turns prospecting into a repeatable motion instead of cold guessing
pros.example: knowing that small lodging properties act after a run of bad connectivity reviews or a brand inspection tells the provider when a call is welcome

cons.claim: Class averages hide large variance inside a class, so a class-level shape can mislead on an individual building
cons.example: two similarly sized restaurants where one is a new-build with open ceilings and conduit and the other is a brick-walled conversion with no path to the back room

cons.claim: Serving many classes at once fragments the offer, the parts inventory and the support pattern before any of them is profitable
cons.example: carrying lodging, food service and residential property deals simultaneously as a two-person shop with one spare of each device

failure_modes: pursuing every venue that answers the phone and ending up with no repeatable shape
treating a property manager like an owner-operator and pitching an on-the-spot decision they cannot make
ignoring who else must consent (landlord, franchisor, building owner) until after a proposal is issued
acceptance_tests: each served class has a written buyer role, demand trigger, footprint driver, consent requirement and at least one disqualifier
revisit_triggers: a class stops converting or starts generating declines at the fit screen
the provider's service radius, staffing or spare inventory changes what it can serve

base.update_signal: conversion or decline patterns by venue class shift, or the provider's serviceable radius changes

nodes.definition: Separate the two reasons a venue pays for Wi-Fi and decide which one is load-bearing for this buyer. The guest story is about the people who visit: coverage at the far booth, the top-floor room or the courtyard, a join experience that does not embarrass the front desk, and the public review or complaint that follows a bad one. The operations story is about the business itself: card terminals, tablet point-of-sale, kitchen display screens, handheld ordering and stock scanners, cloud phone handsets, property-management and door-lock systems, and camera uploads — the systems that stop the venue trading when the network drops. Which story leads decides the message, the tier and often the price basis: guest value sells coverage and appearance and is easy to admire but easy to defer, while operations dependence is usually what justifies paying every month, because it is the difference between an amenity and a utility.

included: the two value narratives and what each is made of
which one carries the recurring fee for a given buyer
how each is stated within evidenced language
excluded: technical separation of guest and operations traffic
measured performance claims about either network

pros.claim: Naming the network the venue cannot trade without focuses the offer on the part a buyer will pay monthly to protect
pros.example: an owner who shrugs at guest coverage signs once it is clear the handheld ordering tablets and the card terminals share one unmanaged failure path

cons.claim: The operations story slides easily into fear-selling and must be held to what the venue's own inventory supports
cons.example: asserting that an outage 'will cost' a specific sum of lost trade is an invented figure, not a value story the provider can stand behind

failure_modes: pitching guest amenity to a buyer whose actual pain is point-of-sale dropouts at peak
using downtime consequences as a scare tactic without the dependency inventory that evidences them
selling a guest-experience tier to a venue whose operations load will break it
acceptance_tests: the offer names which story is load-bearing for this venue and cites the specific systems or guest-facing areas the claim rests on
revisit_triggers: the venue adds or removes a revenue-critical system that changes its dependence
guest-facing expectations change, such as a new patio, an added floor or a booking-site amenity rating

base.update_signal: the venue's dependence profile or guest-facing expectation changes

nodes.definition: Fix, before anything is sold, what the provider will and will not do with the traffic and personal data of people who use a venue's guest network, and put it in the offer in writing. The standing commitments are simple and absolute: no interception, content inspection or browsing-history logging of guest traffic, and no sale, brokerage or secondary marketing use of guest identifiers by the provider. Anything a sign-in page collects — a name, an email address, a room or unit number, a social login — is collected only for a purpose the venue can state out loud, disclosed plainly on that page and in the venue's own notice, kept only as long as that purpose needs, and owned by the venue rather than harvested by the provider. Where a venue wants marketing capture, the answer is disclosure-first and consent-based rather than silent collection, and the governing obligation class — consumer privacy and electronic-marketing notice duties, which differ by jurisdiction and change — is named in the proposal with an instruction to verify current rules locally before the practice is promised.

included: no-interception and no-resale commitments
disclosure-first collection stance and data ownership
the obligation class to verify per jurisdiction
what the provider refuses even when asked
excluded: captive-portal configuration and technical enforcement of network separation
retention practice for the provider's own device-management telemetry

pros.claim: A written privacy stance is both an ethical floor and a real differentiator against vendors whose business model is the guest list
pros.example: a manager who has been pitched free hardware in exchange for guest-data collection can be handed a one-page commitment that the provider never touches guest traffic or sells anything about it

cons.claim: Refusing data monetization removes a revenue line competitors advertise and disappoints venues who want the marketing list
cons.example: a restaurant group that wants portal email capture must be routed through visible disclosure and consent, or told no

failure_modes: agreeing verbally to 'just grab emails at login' with no disclosure to the guest
letting a vendor's default sign-in template collect more than the venue disclosed
treating privacy wording as boilerplate rather than a promise the installed system must honour
acceptance_tests: the proposal contains the no-interception and no-data-resale commitment, names exactly what the sign-in page will collect and why, and states who owns and retains it
any venue request for guest-data collection is recorded together with the disclosure text guests will see and a note to verify current privacy rules in that jurisdiction
revisit_triggers: the venue asks to change what the sign-in page collects or how the data is used
privacy or electronic-marketing rules in the venue's jurisdiction change
a platform vendor changes its default data collection or analytics behaviour

base.update_signal: a privacy rule, a venue data request, or a vendor default that governs guest data changes

nodes.definition: Bound what may be said in a conversation, a quote or a piece of collateral to what the provider can evidence on demand. Coverage and performance statements stay conditional until a survey has been done; uptime, speed and improvement figures are never quoted as facts unless they come from measurements the provider itself took and can show; a competitor's product is described by what it does and does not include rather than by insinuation about competence; and the consequences of poor Wi-Fi are drawn from the venue's own dependency inventory instead of invented loss figures or manufactured urgency about what will happen next weekend. Buyers who are easy to pressure — an owner-operator with no technical staff, an elderly property owner, a franchisee under inspection pressure — get plainer language, an explicit reading of what is excluded, and time to consider, never a same-day signature push or a discount that expires tonight.

included: conditional language before measurement
the ban on unmeasured performance and loss figures
fair description of alternatives
extra care with buyers who are vulnerable to pressure or cannot evaluate the offer technically
excluded: the service-level targets themselves, which the operations knowledge base sets
the technical basis of a coverage prediction

pros.claim: Conditional, evidenced claims survive the survey and the first outage, which is exactly when exaggerated ones destroy an account
pros.example: 'we expect full dining-room and patio coverage subject to survey' can be delivered on; 'guaranteed perfect coverage everywhere' cannot

cons.claim: Careful language sounds weaker beside a competitor who promises certainty, and some deals are lost on that difference alone
cons.example: losing a motel to a bidder who guarantees a speed figure the building's existing cabling cannot carry

failure_modes: quoting an uptime percentage the provider has never measured because it appeared in a manufacturer's brochure
pressing a nervous owner to sign at the table before they have read the exclusions
letting a partner or a subcontractor make a promise in the provider's name that the provider would not make
acceptance_tests: every performance or outcome statement in the collateral is traceable to a measurement the provider holds, a stated assumption, or a manufacturer claim attributed to the manufacturer
the quote states what is excluded in the same document and in the same plain language as what is included
no signature is sought behind a deadline the provider invented, and a buyer with no technical staff has had the exclusions read to them and time to consider before signing
revisit_triggers: a claim in circulation can no longer be evidenced
a partner or subcontractor is found to be selling on promises the provider does not make

base.update_signal: a claim loses its evidence, or a new collateral piece or partner script enters circulation

nodes.definition: Enumerate the classes of permission the work depends on before selling it, because a signed contract for work the provider may not lawfully perform is worse than no contract at all. The classes that recur in this business: contractor or low-voltage licensing for cabling and device installation; electrical and fire-code rules governing cable routing, wall and ceiling penetrations and plenum spaces; permits or inspections that some jurisdictions attach to structured cabling; landlord, lease and property-owner consent for risers, roofs, exterior mounting and shared spaces; franchise or brand technology standards where the venue carries a brand; business registration, general liability insurance and, where staff or subcontractors are used, workers' cover that property managers routinely demand before access; and the consumer-privacy notice duties attached to any guest sign-in page. Each class is named, given a holder — held in-house, subcontracted to a licensed trade, or the venue's own responsibility — and verified as current in that venue's jurisdiction, because these rules vary locally and change, so verification belongs to the deal rather than to a one-time reading.

included: the obligation classes touching install-plus-manage work
who holds each class per deal
the instruction to verify current local rules
insurance and consent artefacts venues demand
excluded: jurisdiction-specific rule text, thresholds or fees
installation practice and code compliance during the build

pros.claim: Deciding who holds each permission class before quoting keeps a signed job from stalling at a lease clause or an inspection
pros.example: discovering that the landlord must approve any riser penetration while the quote is still conditional rather than on the morning of the install

cons.claim: The verification pass costs calendar time and can lose fast deals, and subcontracting a licensed trade compresses the margin
cons.example: a same-week install that has to wait on a property manager's written consent while a competitor promises Friday

failure_modes: assuming a licensing rule read once in one town still applies in the next
promising an installation date before consent and code questions are answered
performing licensed work on the theory that low-voltage cabling never counts
acceptance_tests: every obligation class relevant to the deal has a named holder and a verification note, and any unresolved class is listed as an open condition in the proposal
the venue's insurance and access requirements are collected before an installation date is offered
revisit_triggers: the provider works in a new jurisdiction or takes on a new class of installation work
a landlord, franchisor or insurer changes what it requires before access

base.update_signal: a licensing, permit, insurance or consent requirement changes, or the provider enters a new jurisdiction

nodes.definition: Walk the venue's own operations with the people who run them and write down every system that rides the network and what happens to trade when it stops: card terminals and tablet point-of-sale, kitchen display or expediting screens, handheld ordering and stock-scanning devices, back-office and accounting sessions, cloud phone handsets, door locks and property-management systems in lodging, camera recording and uploads, digital signage and background music, and whatever staff have quietly attached on their own. Each entry records how it connects today, whether it falls back to a cellular path, which vendor owns it, and what the venue does by hand when it is unavailable. This inventory is the factual foundation of the operations value story, the main input to tier choice, and the reason a monthly fee is defensible — and it is discovery rather than persuasion: the provider records what staff report and what it observes, without embellishment, and reflects it back for correction.

included: the inventory of network-dependent systems and their failure consequences
vendor ownership and fallback paths per system
the venue's manual workaround today
excluded: measured device counts and radio load, which the survey establishes
application support for those systems

pros.claim: A dependency list written in the venue's own words replaces sales pressure with a shared picture of what actually breaks
pros.example: a manager who sees that the card terminals, the kitchen screens and the guest network all sit behind one consumer router draws the conclusion without being told

cons.claim: The inventory is a snapshot and venues add devices constantly, so it ages between discovery and installation
cons.example: a self-order kiosk and two tablets added a fortnight after discovery change both the device count and the peak load

failure_modes: accepting 'it is only guest Wi-Fi' without checking what the terminals and back office actually use
inflating the consequences beyond what the venue itself reported
missing a system that fails over to cellular today and will be moved onto the new network later
acceptance_tests: the inventory lists each network-dependent system with its vendor, its connection today, and the venue's stated consequence when it is down, and the venue has confirmed the list
revisit_triggers: the venue adds, replaces or removes a revenue-critical system
the survey reveals devices the staff did not mention

base.update_signal: the venue's set of network-dependent systems changes

nodes.definition: Establish what the venue already has and who has touched it, because that determines the switching cost, the honest comparison and much of the first-year risk. The situations that recur: the internet carrier's supplied gateway doing double duty as the wireless network; a consumer router bought at a big-box store and extended with repeaters; a competent installation from someone who was paid once and has not been seen since; a relative or part-time technician who holds the only administrative credentials; a landlord- or franchise-supplied shared network the venue does not control; or a managed contract that ended badly and left suspicion behind. For each, the audit records who owns the equipment, who holds administrative access and documentation, what remains under warranty or contract, what can be adopted rather than replaced, and what the venue believes is wrong today — and it is completed before any comparison is drawn, so the pitch answers a real situation rather than a caricature.

included: existing equipment, ownership and warranty state
who holds credentials and documentation
contract and shared-network entanglements
what can be adopted versus replaced
excluded: technical assessment of whether existing gear meets the design, which the design knowledge base decides
the transition cutover plan

pros.claim: Knowing who holds the passwords and who owns the equipment stops a signed deal from stalling on access nobody can produce
pros.example: a venue whose only administrative account belongs to a former employee needs a credential-reset and rebuild step priced in before an install date is offered

cons.claim: Auditing an incumbent costs unpaid time and sometimes shrinks the deal by revealing equipment worth keeping
cons.example: finding recent, manageable access points that should be adopted rather than replaced, cutting the hardware line in half

failure_modes: quoting a full replacement before checking what can be adopted
disparaging the previous installer instead of describing the gap in continuing coverage
missing an existing contract or landlord-provided service that constrains what may be changed
acceptance_tests: the audit records equipment ownership, credential holder, documentation state and contract entanglements, and flags anything that must be reset or released before work starts
revisit_triggers: the venue changes internet carrier or is taken over by a new operator
credentials or documentation promised by the venue fail to appear

base.update_signal: the venue's existing equipment, carrier or credential situation changes

nodes.definition: Separate what is genuinely known about a venue from what only an onsite survey can establish, and carry the second group as declared pending facts instead of guesses. The facts that must be seen or measured rather than assumed: construction and interior materials that attenuate signal (masonry, foil-backed insulation, mesh glass, cold rooms, lift shafts), ceiling and mounting conditions, existing cable paths and conduit and whether a switch and power can live where the design needs them, the internet circuit's type and where its demarcation sits, the neighbouring radio environment and congestion in the shared band, outdoor expectations such as patios, courtyards and parking, peak device counts rather than average ones, and the consents attached to risers, roofs and shared spaces. Every item on that list travels into the quote as an explicit assumption with a survey contingency, so that a mid-project revision is a contract mechanism the buyer already agreed to rather than an argument.

included: the list of facts that require a survey
how each is written as an assumption in a quote
the contingency that lets price and promise be revised openly
excluded: how the survey is conducted and how placement is computed
the measurement instruments and validation tests used

pros.claim: Pending facts written as assumptions turn a mid-project change into an agreed mechanism instead of a dispute
pros.example: 'price assumes an existing usable conduit path from the closet to the dining room, confirmed at survey' protects both sides when the conduit turns out to be full

cons.claim: A long assumption list reads as evasive to a buyer who wants a single number today
cons.example: an owner comparing a conditional, itemised quote against a competitor's flat figure with no conditions attached

failure_modes: counting access points off a floor plan and presenting the number as final
assuming a modern circuit and a convenient demarcation position the building does not have
dropping the assumption list from the final proposal to make it look cleaner
acceptance_tests: every quantity in the quote that depends on the building is labelled survey-pending with the assumption it rests on and the contingency that applies if it proves false
revisit_triggers: the survey contradicts an assumption the quote relied on
the venue changes its footprint, adds an outdoor area or renovates before installation

base.update_signal: a survey result, renovation or footprint change converts a pending fact into a firm one or invalidates an assumption

nodes.definition: Write down exactly what the monthly fee performs, and package it into a short ladder of tiers instead of negotiating scope venue by venue. The scope statement names the standing activities — device monitoring and alerting, configuration and firmware upkeep, guest-network hygiene, a stated allowance of moves and changes, a support path with named hours and channels, a periodic health summary, and coordination with the carrier or an equipment vendor when a fault is theirs — and, with equal care, what is not included: new cabling, additional access points, new sites, application support for the venue's point-of-sale or property system, and everything on the far side of the responsibility boundary. Tiers then differ along a few honest dimensions such as support hours, response expectation, whether onsite visits are included or billed, and how many changes are covered, so that a venue with heavy operations dependence buys a higher rung rather than commissioning a bespoke contract nobody can price or repeat.

included: the monthly inclusion and exclusion list
the dimensions along which tiers differ
change allowances and support-hours definitions
excluded: numeric service-level targets and how uptime is measured and reported
the alerting and escalation runbooks that operate the promise

pros.claim: A written inclusion and exclusion list is what turns a support call into a routine ticket instead of a dispute
pros.example: 'adding an access point for the new patio is a change order, not a monthly inclusion' settled in writing before the patio is built

pros.claim: A short tier ladder makes the offer repeatable, quotable and comparable across venues of the same class
pros.example: two restaurants of similar shape can be quoted from the same rung instead of two hand-built agreements

cons.claim: A tight scope can read as ungenerous, and any ladder leaves venues whose real need sits between two rungs
cons.example: a small motel that wants weekend cover but nothing else on the higher tier

failure_modes: saying 'we handle everything' in the meeting and invoking a narrow written scope at the first incident
letting every deal invent its own scope until nothing can be priced or staffed
leaving change allowances undefined so routine requests become unpaid work
acceptance_tests: the scope document lists inclusions and exclusions explicitly and states support hours, response expectation and change allowance per tier
no signed agreement contains a scope item that exists only in conversation
revisit_triggers: the same out-of-scope request recurs across several venues
support load per site diverges from what the tier assumed
a platform change alters what routine upkeep involves

base.update_signal: recurring out-of-scope requests or measured support load change what a tier must contain

nodes.definition: Draw the line, inside the offer, between the internet circuit, the network the provider manages, and the applications riding on top of it — because 'the internet is down' arrives regardless of whose fault it is. The map states that the circuit and the carrier's service belong to the carrier under the venue's own agreement, that everything from the demarcation point inward (gateway, switching, cabling, access points and their configuration) is the managed scope, and that point-of-sale, property-management, camera and phone applications belong to their own vendors. It then states what the provider does anyway when the fault is outside its line: triage first, identify where the fault sits, and where the tier says so, open and chase the third-party ticket on the venue's behalf. Whether the provider also becomes the venue's agent or intermediary for the circuit is a decision made here, with its compensation and its liability understood, rather than drifting into an unpaid obligation nobody agreed to.

included: the carrier, managed-network and application boundaries
the triage and coordination promise across the line
whether the provider acts as the venue's agent for the circuit
excluded: the escalation runbook and third-party ticket handling in live operations
carrier contract negotiation on the venue's behalf

pros.claim: A stated boundary paired with a triage promise gives the venue one number to call without making the provider liable for a carrier outage
pros.example: a cut fibre is identified within the hour, reported to the carrier and explained to the manager, with no service credit owed by the provider

cons.claim: Triage on the venue's behalf consumes real hours for faults the boundary says are not the provider's
cons.example: an hour held in a carrier queue over an outage the provider did not cause and cannot fix

failure_modes: accepting 'one throat to choke' language literally and absorbing carrier failures as service credits
hiding behind the boundary so completely that the venue feels abandoned mid-outage
leaving agency for the circuit undefined and inheriting the carrier relationship by default
acceptance_tests: the agreement names the demarcation point, states which side each component sits on, and describes exactly what the provider does when the fault is on the other side
revisit_triggers: the venue changes carrier, circuit type or demarcation location
recurring outages originate outside the managed boundary and consume unpriced hours

base.update_signal: the venue's carrier arrangement changes or out-of-boundary faults start consuming unpriced time

nodes.definition: Build the monthly number out of components the provider can actually document, rather than from a figure copied off a competitor's website or picked because it sounds acceptable. The mechanism has a per-site part — the standing cost of holding a location, covering the management platform or controller licence attached to the site, monitoring, the share of a support rota, reporting time, and the travel radius the site sits in — and a per-device part, because every managed access point, switch and gateway adds licence cost, alerting surface, upkeep effort and an eventual replacement reserve. Modifiers then reflect support hours, included onsite visits, the number of separate networks to maintain, and the venue's operating hours. Each component is priced from a document the provider holds (a vendor licence quote, its own loaded labour rate, spare-stock cost, insurance premium, vehicle cost), so a quote can be reconstructed line by line, defended, discounted consciously, and re-verified per deal when supplier pricing or the device count moves. What is published to the buyer is the structure and its inputs; no figure is ever presented as a market rate.

included: per-site and per-device components and their modifiers
the cost documents each component is read from
quote validity and per-deal re-verification
excluded: any asserted market price, fee level or margin percentage
billing operations and collections

pros.claim: A cost-built structure lets the provider defend a price, discount deliberately, and see the moment a deal stops paying for the service attached to it
pros.example: showing a buyer that the per-access-point component covers licence, upkeep and a replacement reserve rather than an unexplained 'monitoring' line

cons.claim: Component pricing is harder to sell than one round number and exposes the structure to line-item haggling
cons.example: a buyer trying to strip the reporting component while keeping the response expectation that reporting funds

failure_modes: quoting a monthly figure with no cost basis and discovering the licence renewal alone exceeds it
leaving a quote open after supplier pricing or device counts have moved
hiding travel cost inside a flat fee until the drive time makes the site unprofitable
acceptance_tests: every component of the quoted monthly figure traces to a cost document the provider holds, and the quote carries a validity window and a re-verification note
the quote states the per-site and per-device structure explicitly rather than presenting a single unexplained figure
revisit_triggers: vendor licence, hardware or insurance costs change
the site's device count or operating hours change
discounting becomes routine rather than deliberate

base.update_signal: a supplier quote, labour rate, insurance premium or device count that feeds the structure changes

nodes.definition: Decide, per deal and in writing, who buys the equipment and how its cost is recovered: the venue purchases it outright at installation and owns it; the provider supplies it and recovers the cost through the subscription across a stated period; or the provider retains ownership and the venue effectively rents it for as long as the service runs. Each option moves the upfront objection, the cash the provider must front, the margin profile, the warranty and replacement path, and above all what happens at cancellation — who keeps the access points, whether an unrecovered balance remains, and how a provider-owned device is retrieved or bought out. The choice interacts directly with the contract term, and it also shapes the honest comparison against a one-time installer, since an amortised model looks more expensive per month precisely because it contains equipment the other quote charged for on day one. Whichever is chosen, ownership, warranty route and end-of-term treatment are written into the proposal rather than left to be argued when the relationship is already ending.

included: purchase, amortised and provider-owned options
cancellation and buyout treatment
warranty and replacement routing
cash and margin consequences for the provider
excluded: equipment platform choice and specification
lending, leasing or financing advice for the venue

pros.claim: Amortised or provider-owned equipment removes the upfront barrier that stalls small venues, converting a capital objection into a monthly one
pros.example: a motel that cannot get a lump-sum equipment purchase approved signs a subscription that carries the equipment cost inside it

cons.claim: Fronting equipment ties up the provider's cash and puts recovery at risk if the venue cancels, closes or changes hands early
cons.example: a seasonal venue that shuts after one summer with most of the equipment cost still unrecovered

failure_modes: amortising equipment into a short, freely cancellable term with no recovery clause
leaving ownership ambiguous so the exit becomes a dispute over who keeps the access points
treating a manufacturer warranty as if it were a service level the provider has promised
acceptance_tests: the proposal states who owns the equipment, how its cost is recovered, what happens to it on cancellation, and which warranty path applies to a failed unit
revisit_triggers: equipment or financing costs change materially
early cancellations start leaving unrecovered equipment balances

base.update_signal: equipment cost, supply lead time or the pattern of early cancellations changes

nodes.definition: Structure the commercial terms that hold the subscription together and, just as deliberately, the way it ends. Term length is set by what has to be recovered — equipment, installation labour, onboarding effort — rather than by habit or by what a competitor uses; renewal is stated plainly, including whether the agreement continues month to month or renews for a further term and how much notice either side gives; any price-adjustment mechanism is described by what drives it, such as supplier licence increases or added devices and sites, rather than by an invented percentage; and the exit is written so the venue keeps its own network, with administrative credentials, the current configuration, documentation and any venue-owned equipment handed over on request rather than withheld as leverage. Termination for cause on both sides, transfer when the venue changes hands, and the treatment of any unrecovered equipment complete the structure, so that leaving is a defined process rather than a fight.

included: term length rationale, renewal and notice
price-adjustment mechanism described by its drivers
exit handover of credentials, configuration and documentation
transfer on change of ownership
excluded: retention and renewal campaigns during the life of the account
drafting or reviewing contract language as legal advice

pros.claim: A stated exit that returns credentials and documentation is a trust asset that shortens the signature conversation
pros.example: showing a wary owner the clause that hands back full administrative access and the configuration file on notice

cons.claim: Generous exit terms weaken the security of the recurring book and make equipment amortisation riskier
cons.example: a conversion right to month-to-month that can leave installation and equipment cost unrecovered

failure_modes: auto-renewing for a full further term with no plain-language notice clause the buyer noticed
withholding configuration or credentials to make leaving difficult
leaving change-of-ownership transfer unaddressed in venue classes that change hands often
acceptance_tests: the agreement states term, renewal, notice, what drives any price adjustment, and the handover the venue receives on exit, all in language the signer can read without help
revisit_triggers: cancellations cluster around a particular term or renewal mechanic
a venue changes ownership and the transfer path proves unworkable

base.update_signal: cancellation, renewal or ownership-transfer experience shows a term mechanic is not working

nodes.definition: Test whether the provider can actually deliver the tier it is about to sell at the price it is about to quote, before the signature rather than after. The check estimates the recurring work a site of this shape and dependence will generate — routine upkeep, the support contacts staff of this kind produce, password and device questions, the periodic report, the expected onsite visits and their drive time — and compares that against what remains of the monthly price once licence, spares, insurance and travel components are removed. It then asks the portfolio question: how many sites of this type one technician can hold before the promised response becomes fiction, and whether this venue crosses that line or forces a hire. The output is a decision — sell as quoted, sell a different tier, price the hours or the travel honestly, or decline — and this is the discipline that stops a growing book of monthly revenue from turning into an unserviceable one that churns.

included: estimated recurring effort per site against the price
travel and response feasibility
portfolio capacity per technician
the sell, re-tier or decline decision
excluded: staffing, scheduling and dispatch operations
financial modelling advice for the business as a whole

pros.claim: Catching an unserviceable deal before signing is far cheaper than discovering it during the third night-time callout
pros.example: a venue that trades around the clock an hour beyond the service radius fails the check before it fails the customer

cons.claim: The check runs on estimates that only become real after months of live support, so early numbers are rough and can be too cautious
cons.example: a venue whose staff turnover generates far more password calls than any estimate predicted

failure_modes: selling volume at a price that cannot fund the response the tier promises
ignoring drive time until the technician's week is mostly travel
adding sites past the capacity line because the revenue looks good this month
acceptance_tests: each deal records an estimated monthly effort and travel load against the quoted price, and states whether the current portfolio can absorb the site without breaking the response promise
revisit_triggers: measured support load per site diverges from the estimate
the portfolio approaches the capacity line for a technician or a service radius

base.update_signal: measured support hours, travel time or churn per site type differ from the estimates used

nodes.definition: Shape the offer for food-service venues, where operational dependence is immediate and the environment is unkind to radio. Ordering tablets, card terminals, kitchen screens and handheld devices fail in front of paying customers, so continuity carries the value story and evening and weekend support matters more than anything written about business hours; patios, cellars, thick walls and metal-dense kitchens create coverage expectations that must stay conditional on survey; peak load is a dinner-service phenomenon rather than an average; and the buyer is usually an owner-operator or general manager who is on the floor, decides quickly, watches every fixed cost and cannot approve a large capital purchase in one conversation. The shaped offer therefore leans on an operations-weighted tier, an access-point count driven by dining, bar, patio and service areas rather than square footage alone, guest coverage sold as a supporting benefit, installation windows that respect service times, and a hardware funding option that keeps the day-one number small.

included: food-service dependence profile and peak behaviour
coverage expectations specific to dining, bar and outdoor areas
buyer behaviour, hours and capital constraints
the tier and funding shape that follow
excluded: access-point placement and channel planning for the space
kitchen equipment interference measurement

pros.claim: Aligning support hours with service hours makes the tier choice obvious to a venue that earns its money at night
pros.example: a bar whose worst hour is Friday at nine gets nothing from cover that ends at five, and knows it

cons.claim: Thin margins and seasonality make food-service venues price-sensitive and prone to cancelling in a slow quarter
cons.example: a patio-dependent restaurant reconsidering every fixed monthly cost in the middle of winter

failure_modes: promising patio or courtyard coverage before a survey has looked at the distance and the mounting options
scheduling installation work during service hours and being sent away
selling business-hours support to a venue whose failures happen at night
acceptance_tests: the restaurant offer names the operations systems it protects, states support hours against the venue's trading hours, and marks all coverage claims survey-conditional
revisit_triggers: the venue adds an outdoor area, a kiosk or a delivery-order workflow
trading hours or seasonality change the support pattern

base.update_signal: the venue's layout, trading hours or ordering technology changes

nodes.definition: Shape the offer for motels and small hotels, where guest Wi-Fi is a rated amenity and the operations side is quietly critical at the same time. Coverage is judged room by room by guests who complain publicly, and it appears in booking-site amenity ratings, which gives the guest story unusual commercial weight; meanwhile the property-management system, the door-lock or keycard system, card terminals and front-desk phones ride the same infrastructure. Access-point counts follow room walls, corridor runs and building construction rather than open floor area, older buildings attenuate badly, and long-stay guests streaming in every room shape the load in a way an average device count hides. The buyer is a general manager or owner, often inside a franchise whose brand technology standard must be read and complied with, and capital tends to move on renovation and inspection cycles. The shaped offer prices per site and per access point with a room-count sanity check, states the guest sign-in experience and its privacy commitments explicitly, and stays survey-conditional given how much the building decides.

included: per-room coverage expectation and its review consequences
lodging operations systems on the same infrastructure
brand-standard compliance as a verification step
renovation and inspection buying cycles
excluded: integration engineering with property-management or lock systems
in-room device provisioning design

pros.claim: Lodging pairs a publicly visible guest complaint loop with real back-office dependence, so both value stories point at the same subscription
pros.example: a property whose reviews mention connectivity and whose front desk cannot check guests in during an outage has two reasons to buy the same tier

cons.claim: Older lodging buildings and per-room coverage expectations make these the easiest deals to over-promise and the hardest to satisfy
cons.example: a masonry building where corridor-mounted access points will not carry into every far room without more units than the buyer expected

failure_modes: quoting an access-point count from room count alone in a building that eats signal
promising brand-standard compliance without reading the current brand specification
treating the guest sign-in page as cosmetic when it carries disclosure duties
acceptance_tests: the lodging offer states the coverage basis, the operations systems included, the brand-standard verification step, and what the sign-in page collects and discloses
revisit_triggers: the franchise or brand technology standard is updated
the property renovates, adds a building or changes its property-management system

base.update_signal: brand standards, property layout or the guest-facing sign-in requirement changes

nodes.definition: Shape the offer for multi-dwelling and multi-tenant properties, where the buyer is a property manager or owner and the users are residents or tenants who never chose the provider. Four decisions define the deal: whether the service covers common areas only (lobby, gym, pool, leasing office, corridors) or reaches inside units; who answers a resident who cannot connect, and whether that help desk is included, tiered separately or excluded outright; how any existing bulk-internet or building-wide agreement interacts with what is being sold; and how risers, roofs, shared electrical spaces and unit access constrain the work, all of which needs written owner consent before a date is offered. Resident privacy deserves more care here than anywhere else, because a household's traffic is not a café guest's: the no-interception commitment and any sign-in data practice are stated to the property and, where required, to residents. Any revenue-share or marketing arrangement with the property is disclosed in writing, with its obligation class named and verified locally before money moves.

included: common-area versus in-unit scope decision
resident support ownership
interaction with existing building internet arrangements
consent, access and resident-privacy handling
disclosure of property revenue-share arrangements
excluded: in-unit network engineering and per-unit segmentation design
acting as an internet service provider to residents, which is a different regulated business to verify separately

pros.claim: One property manager can carry several buildings, so a single good relationship multiplies sites without multiplying acquisition effort
pros.example: a manager satisfied with common-area coverage at one building bringing the next two in the portfolio

cons.claim: Resident support demand is the hidden cost that turns a clean common-area contract into an unfunded help desk
cons.example: residents calling the provider directly about their own devices when the contract covered lobby and gym coverage only

failure_modes: leaving resident support ownership unstated and inheriting it by default
starting riser or roof work on verbal permission from someone who cannot grant it
accepting a property's request for visibility into resident traffic
acceptance_tests: the agreement states common-area versus in-unit scope, who supports residents, the written owner consent obtained, and the resident-privacy commitments
any revenue-share or marketing arrangement with the property is written down with its obligation class flagged for local verification
revisit_triggers: the property changes its building-wide internet arrangement or ownership
resident contact volume exceeds what the scope assumed
the property asks for data or visibility the privacy commitment forbids

base.update_signal: property ownership, the building internet arrangement, or resident support volume changes

nodes.definition: Shape the offer for offices and retail shops, the two classes where the network serves staff and transactions rather than an audience. In an office the load is cloud applications, video meetings, desk phones, printers and a visitor network kept apart from the staff one; the buyer is an office manager, practice manager or a principal of a small firm, sometimes alongside an existing technology supplier who should be worked with rather than displaced, and the decision follows a lease, a fit-out or a move. In a retail shop the load is card terminals, inventory and price-check devices, back-office ordering and sometimes brand or franchise requirements about how the store connects; footprints are small, access-point counts are low, and the deal is won on reliability and a support path a shop assistant can actually use without a technical vocabulary. Both are largely weekday-hours venues, which makes standard support hours a fair fit and keeps the tier honest instead of padded with cover nobody needs.

included: office and retail dependence profiles
visitor versus staff network expectations at offer level
buyer roles and their decision triggers
why standard hours usually fit
excluded: desktop, server and application support for the tenant
point-of-sale or line-of-business software administration

pros.claim: Small footprints and weekday hours make these sites cheap to hold, which is what a young portfolio needs between larger deals
pros.example: a professional office of a handful of access points that generates few after-hours calls and predictable upkeep

cons.claim: Low device counts mean low monthly value per site, so acquisition cost and travel can outweigh the subscription
cons.example: a two-access-point shop across town that costs more in drive time than it returns in a quarter

failure_modes: drifting into general computer support because the office has no other technical contact
ignoring a brand or franchise connectivity requirement in a branded retail unit
quoting a site whose travel cost the price structure never absorbed
acceptance_tests: the office or retail offer states which systems are covered, that tenant computer and application support is excluded, and how the site fits the travel and capacity picture
revisit_triggers: the tenant grows, moves or adds locations
requests for general computer support recur and need a written boundary or a priced service

base.update_signal: tenant size, location count or the pattern of support requests changes

nodes.definition: Position the managed offer against what it actually competes with — an installer who is paid once and leaves, and a consumer router configured by whoever was available — without disparaging either. The honest contrast is structural rather than moral: an unmanaged network drifts, because firmware ages, configuration is undocumented, the person who set it up moves on, there are no spares, nobody is watching, and no one is obliged to answer at seven on a Friday evening; the managed offer names who owns each of those duties and what the venue receives every month. Price is compared on contents rather than headline figures, since a lower installation price with no continuing coverage is a different product, and saying that plainly is more persuasive than implying the competitor is incompetent. Where a buyer genuinely wants only an installation, the provider sells that as an installation, with documentation and a clean handover, or declines it — rather than dressing a one-time job up as a subscription or attaching a monthly fee to work it will not perform.

included: the structural contrast between managed and unmanaged outcomes
like-for-like comparison of what each price contains
handling of buyers who want installation only
excluded: claims about a named competitor's reliability or competence
technical benchmarking of competitor equipment

pros.claim: Describing who owns which duty converts a price argument into a scope comparison the managed offer can win on merit
pros.example: setting a one-time installation quote beside a managed quote and marking which line covers firmware upkeep, spares, monitoring and after-hours response

cons.claim: The structural argument takes explanation, and some buyers only compare the first number they see
cons.example: an owner who reads the day-one figure and stops there, never reaching the second year where the comparison inverts

failure_modes: attacking the previous installer personally instead of describing the missing continuing duties
implying that unmanaged equipment fails catastrophically when the honest claim is that it drifts and nobody is watching
accepting an installation-only job and quietly billing a management fee for work not performed
acceptance_tests: the comparison document lists what each option includes and excludes without characterising the competitor, and the installation-only path is offered explicitly where that is what the buyer wants
revisit_triggers: competitors change what their installation price includes
buyers repeatedly misunderstand the comparison, which means it is framed badly

base.update_signal: the local competitive offer set or the typical installation-only package changes

nodes.definition: Assemble the evidence a cautious venue asks for using only things the provider can produce on demand. The legitimate assets: reference venues that have agreed in writing to be named, called or visited; before-and-after measurements the provider actually took at a site it has permission to discuss; an anonymised sample of the monthly health summary the buyer would receive; photographs of the provider's own installations; licences, insurance certificates and manufacturer training credentials; the manufacturer's published specification cited explicitly as the manufacturer's claim rather than the provider's promise; and a plain description of how a support request is answered. Excluded is the entire category of manufactured proof — uptime percentages never measured, savings never calculated, venue logos that are not customers, testimonials nobody gave, and screenshots of someone else's dashboard. A provider with few references says so and offers a pilot, a staged first site or a reference call instead of inventing a track record it will have to defend later.

included: permissioned references and measurements
anonymised sample deliverables
credentials and insurance evidence
how a thin track record is handled honestly
excluded: unmeasured performance statistics of any kind
sharing a customer's data, floor plans or reports without written permission

pros.claim: A sample of the actual monthly deliverable answers 'what do I get for this fee?' better than any adjective
pros.example: handing a prospect an anonymised health summary showing device status, changes made and issues caught that month

cons.claim: Building permissioned proof is slow, and a young provider will lose deals to competitors quoting numbers they cannot support
cons.example: having two reference sites while a rival's brochure claims a percentage no one audits

failure_modes: publishing a customer's name, floor plan or report without written permission
repeating a manufacturer's performance figure as the provider's own promise
assembling a case study from estimates and presenting it as measurement
acceptance_tests: every proof asset in circulation is either permissioned, anonymised, or attributed to its true source, and each can be produced on request
revisit_triggers: a reference customer withdraws permission or leaves
a measurement becomes stale or no longer reflects the current service

base.update_signal: a reference permission, measurement or credential changes or expires

nodes.definition: Work the channels where venue Wi-Fi problems are already visible instead of dialling addresses at random. The productive sources: point-of-sale dealers and payment agents who get blamed when terminals drop; telecom and internet agents selling circuits into the same venues; security and camera integrators whose devices need a network to live on; property managers and lodging suppliers; franchise and brand groups; hospitality, restaurant and merchant associations; electricians and general contractors doing fit-outs; and existing customers with a second site or a neighbour who asks. Each relationship needs its own written terms: what a referral is worth and how and when it is paid, described as a stated arrangement between the two parties rather than an assumed market rate; who talks to the venue and who owns the account and the support relationship afterwards; and — the part that keeps it clean — disclosure to the venue where a fee flows, since referral, commission and disclosure duties vary by jurisdiction and by the partner's own contracts and must be verified before money moves.

included: channels where venue network pain surfaces first
written referral terms and account ownership
disclosure duty and its obligation class
quality expectations set with the partner
excluded: any stated referral amount, rate or percentage
the partner's own regulatory position, which the partner must verify

pros.claim: A partner who is present when the network fails delivers leads already convinced there is a problem worth paying to solve
pros.example: a payment terminal dealer who has just been called out for a fault that was actually the venue's wireless network

cons.claim: Partner-sourced deals arrive with someone else's expectations attached and can be sold on promises the provider would not make
cons.example: a lead told by an integrator that coverage everywhere is included, before any survey or scope conversation

failure_modes: paying or receiving a referral fee that the venue was never told about
letting a partner speak for the provider's scope and pricing without a written brief
leaving account and support ownership ambiguous so the venue does not know who to call
acceptance_tests: each partner relationship has written terms covering fee mechanics, account ownership and support routing, plus a disclosure practice and a note to verify referral and disclosure rules in the relevant jurisdiction
revisit_triggers: a channel starts producing leads that fail the fit screen
a partner's own contracts or regulatory position changes what it may accept
the provider's target venue classes change

base.update_signal: channel yield, partner terms, or disclosure requirements change

nodes.definition: Apply a short written screen before spending survey and proposal effort, and be willing to say no. The disqualifiers that recur in this business: an internet circuit that cannot carry what the venue expects, with no willingness to upgrade it; a landlord, building owner or franchisor whose consent cannot be obtained for the work required; a buyer who wants installation only and no continuing service; a site whose work needs a licence or trade the provider neither holds nor can subcontract; a demand for guarantees that cannot be honoured before a survey, or at all; travel, hours or response expectations the serviceability check cannot fund at any price the buyer would accept; a request to intercept, harvest or resell guest or resident data; and a venue in visible financial distress whose subscription will not survive the quarter. Every decline is recorded with its reason so the pattern becomes visible across a channel or a venue class, and where the blocker is fixable it is offered back as a condition — an upgraded circuit, a written consent, a different tier — rather than as a rejection.

included: the recurring disqualifiers
conditional-yes handling
recording declines with reasons for pattern analysis
excluded: credit assessment or financial advice about the venue
technical feasibility judgements that require the survey

pros.claim: A written screen makes declining a normal act rather than a failure, which protects capacity and reputation at the same time
pros.example: turning down a site that demands a coverage guarantee before survey, and keeping the relationship open with a conditional path

cons.claim: A screen applied too strictly starves a young provider of the deals it needs to build references and cash flow
cons.example: declining a small awkward site that would have produced the first reference in a new venue class

failure_modes: taking a deal that fails the screen because the month has been slow
declining without recording the reason, so the same channel keeps sending the same misfit
treating a fixable blocker as a permanent no and losing a deal that only needed a condition
acceptance_tests: every deal passes or fails a written screen before survey effort is spent, and each decline records its reason and whether a condition could reverse it
revisit_triggers: a disqualifier fires repeatedly from one channel or venue class
the provider's capacity, licensing reach or service radius changes what is now feasible

base.update_signal: decline patterns by channel or venue class, or a change in what the provider can now serve

nodes.definition: Assemble the single document the venue signs and the design work starts from, then gate it before it leaves. A complete proposal states the outcome being bought and the tier that delivers it; the equipment and access-point count as a survey-conditional figure with the assumptions it rests on; the price with its per-site and per-device structure and its exclusions; the equipment ownership and cost-recovery choice; the term, renewal, notice and exit handover; the responsibility boundary and the support path with its hours; the guest-data privacy commitments and anything a sign-in page will collect; the permissions still outstanding and who is obtaining them; and the validity window of the quote. The gate is that nothing ambiguous passes: every survey-pending fact is labelled as such, every exclusion is written where the buyer will read it, the serviceability check has been run and recorded, and each outstanding obligation class has an owner — after which the deal is handed to design and deployment with its assumption list intact rather than as a bare purchase order.

included: the required contents of a signable proposal
the pass conditions that gate it
what is handed to design and deployment
excluded: the design document, placement plan and installation schedule produced afterwards
post-signature project management

pros.claim: One document carrying scope, price structure, assumptions, exclusions and exit terms prevents the whole class of disputes that begin with 'I thought that was included'
pros.example: a venue that later asks for a second building is shown the site-scoped price structure and the change path it already signed

cons.claim: A thorough proposal takes real preparation time and can lose a buyer who wanted a one-page number the same afternoon
cons.example: an owner-operator comparing a complete conditional proposal against a competitor's text message quote

failure_modes: issuing a proposal with an unqualified access-point count and no assumption list
omitting the privacy commitments because the venue did not ask about them
handing design a signed order without the assumptions and open permissions that shaped it
acceptance_tests: the proposal contains scope and tier, survey-conditional quantities with assumptions, price structure and exclusions, equipment ownership, term and exit, responsibility boundary, privacy commitments, outstanding permissions and a validity window
no proposal is issued before the fit screen and the serviceability check have been recorded
revisit_triggers: a survey result contradicts an assumption the signed proposal relied on
recurring post-signature disputes reveal a missing element in the template
term, price structure or privacy commitments change

base.update_signal: a survey contradiction, a post-signature dispute, or a change in terms alters what the proposal must carry

edges.why_related: which venues are worth serving can only be decided once the service being sold is defined
the privacy commitments are part of the product definition rather than an afterthought bolted on at proposal time
what may be claimed follows from what the service actually performs each month
bundling installation with management is what pulls contractor, code, consent and insurance obligation classes into the offer
which value story leads is a property of the venue class before it is a property of the individual site
the class tells the provider which systems to ask about before walking the floor
each class has its own recurring survey-pending facts, from patios and cellars to corridors, risers and stockrooms
the inventory of what breaks decides which tier a venue needs and what the monthly scope must actually cover
the boundary is drawn against a defined scope: it says which side of the line each inclusion and exclusion sits on
a price can only be built once the work the fee performs is written down
device counts, cabling paths and travel distance are the pending facts the per-device and per-site components multiply
how equipment cost is recovered is a decision inside the price structure, not beside it
the term has to be long enough to recover whatever the provider fronted, and the exit has to say what happens to it
serviceability is tested against the specific price the structure produced for this site
office and retail offers are shaped almost entirely by which staff and transaction systems ride the network
the comparison must answer the venue's real existing arrangement rather than a generic caricature of one
a site that cannot be served at any acceptable price is a decline, and the screen needs that verdict to fire
proposal effort is spent only on deals that have passed the screen, and the screen's conditions become proposal conditions
the proposal may not offer a data practice the privacy commitment forbids, and must state what a sign-in page collects
